Continuous order-to-order quantum phase transitions from fixed-point annihilation

Journal: Rep. Prog. Phys.
David J. Moser    Lukas Janssen Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik and Würzburg-Dresden Cluster of Excellence ct.qmat, TU Dresden, 01062 Dresden, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

A central concept in the theory of phase transitions beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm is fractionalization: the formation of new quasiparticles that interact via emergent gauge fields. This concept has been extensively explored in the context of continuous quantum phase transitions between distinct orders that break different symmetries. We propose a mechanism for continuous order-to-order quantum phase transitions that operates independently of fractionalization. This mechanism is based on the collision and annihilation of two renormalization group fixed points: a quantum critical fixed point and an infrared stable fixed point. The annihilation of these fixed points rearranges the flow topology, eliminating the disordered phase associated with the infrared stable fixed point and promoting a second critical fixed point, unaffected by the collision, to a quantum critical point between distinct orders. We argue that this mechanism is relevant to a broad spectrum of physical systems. In particular, it can manifest in Luttinger fermion systems in three spatial dimensions, leading to a continuous quantum phase transition between an antiferromagnetic Weyl semimetal state, which breaks time-reversal symmetry, and a nematic topological insulator, characterized by broken lattice rotational symmetry. This continuous antiferromagnetic-Weyl-to-nematic-insulator transition might be observed in rare-earth pyrochlore iridates R2R_{2}Ir2O7. Other possible realizations include kagome quantum magnets, quantum impurity models, and quantum chromodynamics with supplemental four-fermion interactions.

1 Introduction

The exploration of quantum phase transitions beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm [1, 2] has garnered significant attention in recent years. A particular focus has been on continuous quantum phase transitions between phases that break different symmetries [3]. Traditionally, it has been believed that such transitions require fractionalization, where new “deconfined” quasiparticles with fractional quantum numbers arise and interact via emergent gauge fields. The intense study of deconfined quantum phase transitions in recent years has significantly advanced our understanding of quantum critical phenomena. Notable insights include the discovery of emergent symmetries [4, 5, 6, 7], the identification of spectroscopic signatures of fractionalization [8], the uncovering of unexpected webs of field-theoretical dualities [9], and the observation of anomalous scaling behaviors in entanglement entropy [10, 11]. However, the most recent numerical studies suggest that the deconfined quantum phase transition, at least in its original formulation within SU(2) spin models [1, 2, 3], is ultimately first-order, characterized by a finite, though large, correlation length at the transition point [12, 6, 13, 14, 11].

Here, we propose a mechanism that provides a different pathway to continuous order-to-order quantum phase transitions, one that does not rely on fractionalization. Our proposal involves the collision and annihilation of two renormalization group (RG) fixed points: a quantum critical fixed point and an infrared stable fixed point. We argue that the mechanism is relevant to a broad spectrum of physical systems. In particular, we explicitly demonstrate within a RG calculation that three-dimensional Luttinger fermion systems undergo a continuous quantum phase transition between an antiferromagnetic Weyl semimetal state, marked by broken time-reversal symmetry, and a nematic topological insulator state, characterized by broken lattice rotational symmetry. Further possible realizations in other setups are discussed as well.

The mechanism is schematically illustrated in Fig. 1, which shows RG flow diagrams for two different values of an external control parameter NN. For NN larger than a critical value NcN_{\mathrm{c}}, there is an interacting disordered phase, which is separated from two ordered phases by continuous phase transition lines, see Fig. 1(a). As NN decreases, the fixed point associated with the disordered phase (D) and those governing one of the two transition lines (QCP2) approach each other and eventually collide at a critical value NcN_{\mathrm{c}}. For NN smaller than NcN_{\mathrm{c}}, Fig. 1(b), the fixed-point annihilation alters the flow topology by removing the disordered phase, leaving behind a continuous phase transition line between two phases with distinct orders. Note that the QCP1 fixed point, which governs the resulting continuous order-to-order transition, is entirely decoupled from the fixed-point annihilation occurring between D and QCP2. On the left-hand side of QCP1, for G1G_{1} below the fixed-point value, the system would naturally flow toward the disordered phase. However, due to the annihilation of the disordered fixed point D with QCP2, this phase becomes unstable, giving rise instead to the competing order. Notably, since the proposed mechanism solely relies on the fixed-point annihilation of the fixed points D and QCP2 and the resulting rearrangement of the flow topology, any quantum critical fixed point not involved in the annihilation qualifies as QCP1.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: In Sec. 2, we discuss in detail a concrete realization of the proposed mechanism in Luttinger fermion systems in three spatial dimensions, relevant to certain pyrochlore iridates. Another potential realization, pertinent to kagome quantum magnets, is discussed in Sec. 3. We conclude with a summary of results in Sec. 4. The appendices provide technical details of the calculations and discuss additional potential realizations of the mechanism in quantum impurity models and quantum chromodynamics.

2 Pyrochlore iridates

2.1 Model

We begin by reviewing the interacting Luttinger fermion model in three spatial dimensions [15, 16, 17, 18]. This continuum model effectively describes electronic excitations near a quadratic band touching point at the Fermi level, as they occur in pyrochlore iridates R2R_{2}Ir2O7, with RR a rare-earth element [19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. In the low-temperature limit, the model can be defined by the Euclidean action S=S0+SintS=S_{0}+S_{\text{int}}, where S0S_{0} corresponds to the noninteracting part,

S0=∫dτd3x→∑i=1Nψi†(∂τ+∑a=15(1+saδ)da(−ⅈ∇)γa)ψi,\displaystyle S_{0}=\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential{\tau}\differential[3]{\vec x}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\psi^{\dagger}_{i}\left(\partial_{\tau}+\sum_{a=1}^{5}(1+s_{a}\delta)d_{a}(-\rmi\nabla)\gamma_{a}\right)\psi_{i}, (1)

which originates in the Luttinger Hamiltonian [24]. In the above, NN corresponds to the number of band touching points at the Fermi level, with N=1N=1 in the case of the pyrochlore iridates, ψi\psi_{i} is a four-component Grassmann field, sa≔1s_{a}\coloneqq 1 (sa≔−1s_{a}\coloneqq-1) for a=1,2,3a=1,2,3 (a=4,5a=4,5), δ\delta parametrizes the cubic anisotropy with −1≤δ≤1-1\leq\delta\leq 1, the 4×44\times 4 matrices γa\gamma_{a} fulfill the Euclidean Clifford algebra, {γa,γb}=2​δa​b​𝟙\{\gamma_{a},\gamma_{b}\}=2\delta_{ab}\mathbbm{1}, and d1​(p→)≔3​py​pzd_{1}(\vec{p})\coloneqq\sqrt{3}p_{y}p_{z}, d2​(p→)≔3​px​pzd_{2}(\vec{p})\coloneqq\sqrt{3}p_{x}p_{z}, d3​(p→)≔3​px​pyd_{3}(\vec{p})\coloneqq\sqrt{3}p_{x}p_{y}, d4​(p→)≔3​(px2−py2)/2d_{4}(\vec{p})\coloneqq\sqrt{3}(p_{x}^{2}-p_{y}^{2})/2, and d5​(p→)≔(2​pz2−px2−py2)/2d_{5}(\vec{p})\coloneqq(2p_{z}^{2}-p_{x}^{2}-p_{y}^{2})/2 are proportional to the ℓ=2\ell=2 real spherical harmonics.

We account for both short-range repulsion and the long-range tail of the Coulomb interaction via [25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31]

Sint\displaystyle S_{\text{int}} =−∫dτdx→{G12​N(ψ†γ45ψ)2+G22​N∑a=15(ψ†γaψ)2\displaystyle=-\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential{\tau}\differential[]\vec{x}\,\biggl\{\frac{G_{1}}{2N}(\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{45}\psi)^{2}+\frac{G_{2}}{2N}\sum_{a=1}^{5}(\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{a}\psi)^{2}
+e28​π​N∫d3y→ψ†(x→)ψ(x→)1|x→−y→|ψ†(y→)ψ(y→)},\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt+\frac{e^{2}}{8\pi N}\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential[3]{\vec y}\psi^{\dagger}(\vec{x})\psi(\vec{x})\frac{1}{|\vec{x}-\vec{y}|}\psi^{\dagger}(\vec{y})\psi(\vec{y})\biggr\}, (2)

where we defined γ45≔ⅈ​γ4​γ5\gamma_{45}\coloneqq\rmi\gamma_{4}\gamma_{5}. For notational simplicity, we abbreviated ψ≡ψi​(τ,x→)\psi\equiv\psi_{i}(\tau,\vec{x}) and ψ⁡(x→)≡ψi​(τ,x→)\psi(\vec{x})\equiv\psi_{i}(\tau,\vec{x}), and suppressed the summation symbols over i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N. The long-range tail parameterized by the charge e2e^{2} must be taken into account because the Coulomb interaction is only marginally screened due to the vanishing density of states at the Fermi level [28]. The coupling G1G_{1} originates from local Hubbard repulsion [32], and is believed to increase with decreasing radius of the rare-earth ion [19]. As we show below, a sizable G1G_{1} generates a transition towards a Weyl semimetal phase characterized by spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking and all-in-all-out (AIAO) antiferromagnetic order on the pyrochlore lattice [27, 30, 32, 31]. The coupling G2G_{2} may be assumed to be small on the microscopic level. However, as will be shown below, G2G_{2} is generated by G1G_{1} and the long-range interaction, and we therefore include it from the outset. A sizable G2G_{2} drives a transition towards a nematic phase characterized by spontaneous lattice rotational symmetry breaking and a topological gap in the fermionic spectrum [25, 26, 29]. While previous works have focused exclusively on instabilities toward either AIAO order [27, 30, 32, 31] or nematic order [25, 26, 29], the present study treats both order parameters on equal footing. This proves essential for revealing the direct order-to-order transition.

2.2 Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation

It is convenient to rewrite the interactions in the Luttinger model in terms of Hubbard-Stratonovich fields aa, ϕ\phi, and φ\varphi. In particular, this formulation is crucial in order to explicitly compute order parameters within the RG approach, since it avoids the runaway flows encountered in the purely fermionic formulations [25, 29, 30].

We introduce the scalar Coulomb field aa via

Sa=∫dτ​d3x→​[12​(∇a)2+ⅈ​eN​a​ψi†​ψi],\displaystyle S_{a}=\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential{\tau}\differential[3]{\vec x}\left[\frac{1}{2}(\nabla a)^{2}+\frac{\rmi e}{\sqrt{N}}a\psi^{\dagger}_{i}\psi_{i}\right], (3)

where the summation over repeated indices i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N has been implicitly assumed. All-in-all-out (AIAO) fluctuations are parametrized by an Ising order-parameter field ϕ\phi, which couples to the electronic quasiparticles as [27, 30, 32, 31]

Sϕ=∫dτ​d3x→​[12​ϕ​(r1−∇2)​ϕ+g1N​ϕ​ψi†​γ45​ψi],\displaystyle S_{\phi}=\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential{\tau}\differential[3]{\vec x}\left[\frac{1}{2}\phi(r_{1}-\nabla^{2})\phi+\frac{g_{1}}{\sqrt{N}}\phi\psi^{\dagger}_{i}\gamma_{45}\psi_{i}\right], (4)

where r1r_{1} represents the tuning parameter for the AIAO transition and g1g_{1} is the AIAO Yukawa coupling. Nematic fluctuations are parametrized by a five-component tensor order-parameter field φa\varphi_{a}, which couples to the electronic quasiparticles as [26, 28, 29]

Sφ=∫dτd3x→[12∑a=15φa(r2−c∂τ2−∇2)φa\displaystyle S_{\varphi}=\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential{\tau}\differential[3]{\vec x}\Biggl[\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a=1}^{5}\varphi_{a}(r_{2}-c\partial_{\tau}^{2}-\nabla^{2})\varphi_{a}
+g2N∑a=15φaψi†γaψi+λN∑a,b,c=15tr⁡(Λa​Λb​Λc)φaφbφc],\displaystyle+\frac{g_{2}}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{a=1}^{5}\varphi_{a}\psi^{\dagger}_{i}\gamma_{a}\psi_{i}+\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{a,b,c=1}^{5}\tr( \Lambda_a \Lambda_b \Lambda_c )\varphi_{a}\varphi_{b}\varphi_{c}\biggr]\,, (5)

where r2r_{2} represents the tuning parameter for the nematic transition, g2g_{2} is the nematic Yukawa coupling, and λ\lambda parametrizes the bosonic self-interaction. Λa\Lambda_{a} denote the five real Gell-Mann matrices in three spatial dimensions.11 1 We follow the notation of Ref. [31]. The five real Gell-Mann matrices, and therefore also the ℓ=2\ell=2 real spherical harmonics used in Ref. [26] correspond to the ones used here by relabelling indices (1,2,3,4,5)↦(4,3,2,1,5)(1,2,3,4,5)\mapsto(4,3,2,1,5). The parameter cc is power-counting irrelevant and included for regularization purposes. Quartic bosonic self-interactions are also power-counting irrelevant and are therefore set to zero from the beginning.

The fermion-boson model defined by the Euclidean action

SFB=S0+Sa+Sϕ+Sφ\displaystyle S_{\text{FB}}=S_{0}+S_{a}+S_{\phi}+S_{\varphi} (6)

is quadratic in the Hubbard-Stratonovich fields aa, ϕ\phi, and φ\varphi. The latter can therefore, in principle, be integrated out. The original microscopic, purely fermionic action S=S0+SintS=S_{0}+S_{\text{int}} presented in the main text can then be recovered from the above fermion-boson action in the limit of infinite order-parameter masses r1,2→∞r_{1,2}\to\infty and g1,22→∞g_{1,2}^{2}\to\infty, with fixed ratios

G1=g12r1andG2=g22r2,\displaystyle G_{1}=\frac{g_{1}^{2}}{r_{1}}\hskip 20.00003pt\text{and}\hskip 20.00003ptG_{2}=\frac{g_{2}^{2}}{r_{2}}, (7)

and with c=λ=0c=\lambda=0.

2.3 Mean-field theory

In the large-NN limit and for small G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, the couplings flow to an infrared stable RG fixed point, characterizing an interacting semimetal phase. This phase, which realizes a three-dimensional non-Fermi liquid, is known as the Luttinger-Abrikosov-Beneslavskii (LAB) phase [15, 16, 17]. Sizable four-fermion interactions beyond a finite threshold, however, drive instabilities of the LAB state, which can be understood within a mean-field analysis. To this end, we integrate out the fermion fields ψi†\psi^{\dagger}_{i} and ψi\psi_{i}, i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N, in Eq. (6), leading to an effective action for the Hubbard-Stratonovich fields. In the large-NN limit, the saddle point of this effective action dominates the partition function. Determining the saddle-point solution ultimately reduces to minimizing the mean-field energy [26, 33, 31],

EMF​(ϕ,φ)\displaystyle E_{\text{MF}}(\phi,\varphi) =r12​ϕ2+r22​φ2\displaystyle=\frac{r_{1}}{2}\phi^{2}+\frac{r_{2}}{2}\varphi^{2}
+N∫0Λd3p→(2​π)3[εϕ,φ+(p→)+εϕ,φ−(p→)]\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt+N\int_{0}^{\Lambda}\hskip-2.5pt\frac{\differential[3]{\vec p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\left[\varepsilon_{\phi,\varphi}^{+}(\vec{p})+\varepsilon_{\phi,\varphi}^{-}(\vec{p})\right] (8)

with respect to the order-parameter fields ϕ\phi and φ\varphi. Here, we used the fact that minimization of the mean-field energy implies the Coulomb field vanishes at the mean-field level, and assumed that the nematic order parameter takes the form (φa)=(0,0,0,0,φ)(\varphi_{a})=(0,0,0,0,\varphi). This form implies that the nematic phase is uniaxial, characterized by a single director with a residual discrete rotational symmetry remaining intact in the plane perpendicular to the director, and is believed to realize the smallest mean-field energy among the different possible nematic states [26]. Λ\Lambda is the ultraviolet cutoff. The integrands εϕ,φ±​(p→)\varepsilon^{\pm}_{\phi,\varphi}(\vec{p}) denote the two lower-branch energy eigenvalues of the mean-field Hamiltonian HMF=∑a=15(1+sa​δ)​da​(p→)​γa+g1N​ϕ​γ45+g2N​φ​γ5H_{\text{MF}}=\sum_{a=1}^{5}(1+s_{a}\delta)d_{a}(\vec{p})\gamma_{a}+\frac{g_{1}}{\sqrt{N}}\phi\gamma_{45}+\frac{g_{2}}{\sqrt{N}}\varphi\gamma_{5}. They are given as

εϕ,φ±​(p→)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\phi,\varphi}^{\pm}(\vec{p}) =−\bBigg@3.5[(1−δ)2p4+4δ∑a=13da2(p→)+(g1​ϕN)2+(g2​φN)2\displaystyle=-\bBigg@{3.5}[(1-\delta)^{2}p^{4}+4\delta\sum_{a=1}^{3}d_{a}^{2}(\vec{p})+\left(\tfrac{g_{1}\phi}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^{2}+\left(\tfrac{g_{2}\varphi}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^{2}

Importantly, I5/2(α,δ=−1/2)>0I_{5/2}(\alpha,\delta=-1/2)>0 for all values of α\alpha. This implies a continuous transition between the disordered Luttinger semimetal and the long-range-ordered phases, such that the higher-order terms 𝒪⁡(χ3)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{3}) in Eq. (11) can be neglected near the transition. In order to determine the nature of the transition between the two ordered phases, it is useful to rescale the fields ϕ\phi and φ\varphi in a way that the coefficient of the nonanalytic term in the AIAO sector is the same as those in the nematic sector. This can be achieved by introducing the rescaled polar angle α¯\overline{\alpha} using the field redefinitions ϕ=[N/(a1​g1)]​χ​cos⁡α¯\phi=[\sqrt{N}/(a_{1}g_{1})]\chi\cos\overline{\alpha} and φ=[N/(a2​g2)]​χ​sin⁡α¯\varphi=[\sqrt{N}/(a_{2}g_{2})]\chi\sin\overline{\alpha} with a1≔[I5/2​(α=0)]2/5a_{1}\coloneqq[I_{5/2}(\alpha=0)]^{2/5} and a2≔[I5/2​(α=π/2)]2/5a_{2}\coloneqq[I_{5/2}(\alpha=\pi/2)]^{2/5}. Note that α=α¯\alpha=\overline{\alpha} for α∈{0,π/2,π,3​π/2}\alpha\in\{0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2\}. On the level of the quadratic term ∝χ2\propto\chi^{2} in the mean-field energy, the rescaling can be absorbed in a redefinition of the tuning parameters r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}. The rescaled coefficient of the nonanalytic term ∝χ5/2\propto\chi^{5/2} now takes the form

I5/2¯​(α¯,δ)\displaystyle\overline{I_{5/2}}(\overline{\alpha},\delta) ≔(cos2​α¯a12+sin2​α¯a22)5/4​I5/2​(α⁡(α¯),δ).\displaystyle\coloneqq\left(\frac{\cos^{2}\overline{\alpha}}{a_{1}^{2}}+\frac{\sin^{2}\overline{\alpha}}{a_{2}^{2}}\right)^{5/4}I_{5/2}(\alpha(\overline{\alpha}),\delta)\,. (15)

Figure 2(b) shows I5/2¯\overline{I_{5/2}} as function of α¯\overline{\alpha} for a representative fixed value of δ=−1/2\delta=-1/2. The rescaled coefficient hosts three global minima, lying at angles α¯=0,π\overline{\alpha}=0,\pi (AIAO sector) as well as α¯=π/2\overline{\alpha}=\pi/2 (nematic sector). This implies that a coexistence phase (corresponding to α∉{0,π/2,π,3​π/2}\alpha\notin\{0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2\}) is not realized for all values of r1′r_{1}^{\prime} and r2′r_{2}^{\prime}. As a consequence, the mean-field theory predicts a direct discontinuous transition between the AIAO and nematic orders.

This analytical result is consistent with the numerical minimization of the mean-field energy, Eq. (11), with respect to the mean-field parameters χ\chi and α\alpha for given G1=g12/r1G_{1}=g_{1}^{2}/r_{1}, G2=g22/r2G_{2}=g_{2}^{2}/r_{2}, and δ\delta. This is illustrated in Fig. 3(a), which shows the resulting mean-field phase diagram as function of G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} for a fixed representative value of δ\delta. Beyond the LAB phase at small couplings, we identify two ordered phases: For sufficiently large G1G_{1}, a Weyl semimetal phase emerges, characterized by the Ising order parameter ⟨ϕ⟩∝⟨ψ†​γ45​ψ⟩\langle\phi\rangle\propto\langle\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{45}\psi\rangle, which signals spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking. On the pyrochlore lattice, this phase exhibits all-in-all-out (AIAO) antiferromagnetic order [27, 30, 31]. In contrast, for sizable G2G_{2}, we find a nonmagnetic phase that breaks lattice rotational symmetry. This phase is characterized by the nematic order parameter ⟨φ⟩∝⟨ψ†​γ5​ψ⟩\langle\varphi\rangle\propto\langle\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{5}\psi\rangle, constructed from one of the five irreducible components of traceless symmetric tensors in three dimensions [26]. It corresponds to a nematic topological insulator [25, 29]. While the transitions from the LAB phase to the ordered phases are continuous, the direct transition between the two ordered phases is first order, consistent with the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm.

2.4 RG analysis

At finite NN, fluctuation effects can become significant. To account for these effects, we use an RG analysis in the dynamical bosonization framework [34, 35, 36]. This approach applies a Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation after each RG step, effectively capturing potential nonperturbative effects from the RG-induced generation of four-fermions couplings while avoiding the unphysical singularities associated with their runaway flow. The method has been successfully applied to Luttinger semimetals [29], demonstrating the existence of a critical value NcN_{\mathrm{c}} of quadratic band touching points at the Fermi level, consistent with earlier analyses [25, 28]. For N↘NcN\searrow N_{\mathrm{c}}, the infrared stable fixed point corresponding to the LAB phase collides and annihilates with the quantum critical fixed point that governs the transition between the LAB phase and the nematic topological insulator. All the different approaches predict a value of NcN_{\mathrm{c}} around 22, and therewith above the physical case N=1N=1 relevant for the pyrochlore iridates.

Crucially, the dynamically bosonized RG approach allows us to compute the order parameters as functions of the microscopic couplings by integrating out the RG flow. This enables us to determine the nature of the phase transitions explicitly.

2.4.1 4−ϵ4-\epsilon expansion.

To begin with, note that the fermion-boson model defined in Eq. (6) features a unique upper critical dimension. This is because the effective charge ee, the AIAO Yukawa coupling g1g_{1}, the nematic Yukawa coupling g2g_{2}, and the nematic self-interaction λ\lambda become simultaneously marginal in d=4d=4 spatial dimensions. The presence of a unique upper critical dimension enables a controlled 4−ϵ4-\epsilon expansion. To generalize our theory to noninteger spatial dimensions 2<d<42<d<4, we maintain the general dimensional scaling of the couplings, but perform angular integrations directly in the physical dimension d=3d=3 [37]. This approach is considered the most suitable for models of this type [26]. The dimensionless functions fi​(δ)f_{i}(\delta) are defined in A. Note that the self-energy contributions to the flow of e2e^{2}, depicted in Figs. 4(a)-(c), cancel with the explicit charge vertex renormalizations, shown in Figs. 4(h)-(j), as a consequence of the Ward identity associated with the minimalistic gauge transformation ψ↦ⅇⅈ​e​λ​(τ)​ψ\psi\mapsto\rme^{\rmi e\lambda(\tau)}\psi, a↦a−∂τλ⁡(τ)a\mapsto a-\partial_{\tau}\lambda(\tau) [29, 31]. The parameter cc is an irrelevant parameter that is kept in order to regularize purely bosonic loops in the nematic sector, shown in Figs. 4(g) and 4(s). Note that such regularization parameter is not required in the AIAO sector [31], since a cubic bosonic self-interaction is forbidden by the Ising symmetry of the AIAO order parameter field ϕ\phi. In the above, we have expanded the flow equations assuming small c≪1c\ll 1. As will be shown in Sec. 2.4.3, this assumption is consistent with cc being small at all fixed points of interest, namely, the LAB fixed point, the nematic fixed point, and the AIAO fixed point.

Following Ref. [29], we neglect the anomalous contribution ∝∑i,j,k=1d∂iTi​j​∂kTk​j\propto\sum_{i,j,k=1}^{d}\partial_{i}T_{ij}\partial_{k}T_{kj} in the nematic sector, allowed whenever the spatial dimension dd agrees with dimT\dim T, the dimension of the nematic tensor field Ti​j=∑a=1(d−1)​(d+2)/2φa​Λa,i​jT_{ij}=\sum_{a=1}^{(d-1)(d+2)/2}\varphi_{a}\Lambda_{a,ij}.

For simplicity, the flow equations for the nematic Yukawa coupling g22g_{2}^{2}, the self-interaction coupling λ\lambda, the regularization parameter cc, and the nematic tuning parameter r2r_{2} have further been expanded to lowest order in the anisotropy parameter δ\delta around the isotropic case δ=0\delta=0. This is sufficient to describe the nematic sector, see Sec. 2.4.3. For consistency, before any rescalings of coupling constants, also the involved anomalous dimensions ηψ\eta_{\psi} and ηφ\eta_{\varphi} and the dynamical exponent zz have to be expanded to their leading orders in δ\delta in these cases, ηψ(0)=ηψ|δ=0\eta_{\psi}^{(0)}=\eta_{\psi}\big|_{\delta=0}, ηφ(0)=ηφ|δ=0\eta_{\varphi}^{(0)}=\eta_{\varphi}\big|_{\delta=0}, and z(0)=z|δ=0z^{(0)}=z\big|_{\delta=0}. Note, however, that anisotropy-dependent coupling reparametrizations, such as the above rescaling (e2,g12)↦(1−δ2)​(e2,g12)(e^{2},g_{1}^{2})\mapsto(1-\delta^{2})(e^{2},g_{1}^{2}), can still lead to crucial anisotropy dependencies. On the level of the 4−ϵ4-\epsilon expansion, this happens explicitly through two vertex corrections in the flow equation of g22g_{2}^{2} now involving a factor of 1−δ21-\delta^{2} and implicitly in the flow equations of g22g_{2}^{2}, λ\lambda, and cc through the reparametrized anomalous dimension ηψ(0)\eta_{\psi}^{(0)} involving a factor of 1−δ21-\delta^{2}, see Eq. (26). In general, the theory space is spanned by 13 different parameters, namely the anisotropy parameter δ\delta, the effective charge ee, the AIAO Yukawa coupling g1g_{1}, the AIAO tuning parameter r1r_{1}, two nematic Yukawa couplings g2,tg_{2,\text{t}} and g2,eg_{2,\text{e}} (associated with the T2​g\text{T}_{2\text{g}} and Eg\text{E}_{\text{g}} components of the nematic tensor order parameter), three cubic nematic self-interactions λttt\lambda_{\text{t}\text{t}\text{t}}, λtte\lambda_{\text{t}\text{t}\text{e}}, and λeee\lambda_{\text{e}\text{e}\text{e}}, two regularization parameters ctc_{\text{t}} and cec_{\text{e}}, and two nematic tuning parameters r2,tr_{2,\text{t}} and r2,er_{2,\text{e}}. Note that T2​g⊗Eg⊗Eg=2​T1​g⊕2​T2​g\text{T}_{2\text{g}}\otimes\text{E}_{\text{g}}\otimes\text{E}_{\text{g}}=2\text{T}_{1\text{g}}\oplus 2\text{T}_{2\text{g}} [38], which forbids terms like φ1​φ4​φ5\varphi_{1}\varphi_{4}\varphi_{5} in the action. This implies the absence of a fourth cubic self-interaction governed by a coupling λtee\lambda_{\text{t}\text{e}\text{e}}. Expanding the flow in the nematic sector around the isotropic limit allows us to restrict the parameter space to an eight-dimensional subspace spanned by δ\delta, ee, g1g_{1}, r1r_{1}, g2g_{2}, λ\lambda, cc, and r2r_{2}. The cost of this simplification is the introduction of an additional free parameter c1c_{1} in the flow of the nematic Yukawa coupling g2g_{2}. However, the contribution involving c1c_{1} is merely a biquadratic term, ∝g12​g22\propto g_{1}^{2}g_{2}^{2}. As such, we can already anticipate that its impact on the flow will likely be quantitative rather than qualitative. Indeed, as will be shown in Sec. 2.4.3, both the location as well as the scaling exponents of the LAB fixed point, the nematic fixed point, and the AIAO fixed point remain entirely unaffected by the value of c1c_{1}. We therefore expect that disregarding the distinction between the T2​g\text{T}_{2\text{g}} and Eg\text{E}_{\text{g}} components of the nematic tensor order parameter will not affect the universal physics. For the numerical integration of the flow equations presented in Sec. 2.4.4, we choose c1≡1/5c_{1}\equiv 1/5, which represents the weighted average of the T2​g\text{T}_{2\text{g}} and Eg\text{E}_{\text{g}} contributions c1t=+1c_{\text{1t}}=+1 and c1e=−1c_{\text{1e}}=-1.

The flow equations presented here generalize those previously derived for the individual AIAO [31] and nematic [29] sectors, reducing to these in the respective limits.

2.4.2 Dynamical bosonization scheme.

In three spatial dimensions, it is no longer sufficient to solely work with the flow equations arising from the 4−ϵ4-\epsilon expansion. Additionally, we need to take into account four-fermion box diagrams, which generate further four-fermion interactions, not present at the microscopic scale. These are shown at the one-loop order in Fig. 5. Although these contributions can be safely neglected for small ϵ=4−d≪1\epsilon=4-d\ll 1, four-fermion contributions to the nematic channel turn out to be crucial in 2<d<42<d<4  [29]. Neglecting these contributions would mask the fixed-point collision and annihilation of the LAB fixed point with the nematic fixed point when lowering the number of quadratic band touching points NN below a critical flavor number NcN_{\text{c}}. Using dynamical bosonization in the nematic sector, RG-generated four-fermion interactions can be directly incorporated into the flow of the nematic Yukawa coupling g22g_{2}^{2} [34, 35, 36, 39, 29]. To illustrate this, consider the renormalized action

Note that although the four-fermion interaction is absent in the ultraviolet, it gets generated under an RG transformation. 2.4.3 Fixed-point structure.

We now discuss the fixed-point structure of the model. Based on the mean-field results, we expect that in the large-NN limit, the system exhibits a fully infrared stable fixed point corresponding to the disordered LAB phase [15, 16, 17], along with two quantum critical fixed points associated with instabilities toward AIAO [27, 30, 31] and nematic [25, 26, 29] order, respectively. For finite NN, however, we explicitly show below that the LAB fixed point collides (annihilates) with the nematic fixed point at (below) a critical number of quadratic band touching points Nc>1N_{\text{c}}>1. Moreover, we demonstrate that the AIAO fixed point does not take part in the collision and annihilation process, but remains in the physical space of real couplings for any number of quadratic band touching points N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}.

To observe the fixed-point annihilation at finite coupling strengths, it is convenient to reparametrize the AIAO Yukawa coupling g12↦g12/(−δ)g_{1}^{2}\mapsto g_{1}^{2}/(-\delta) and the corresponding AIAO tuning parameter r1↦r1/(−δ)r_{1}\mapsto r_{1}/(-\delta). Additionally, we introduce the new tuning variables

α1\displaystyle\alpha_{1} ≔r11+r1,\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{r_{1}}{1+r_{1}}, α2\displaystyle\alpha_{2} ≔r21+r2,\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{r_{2}}{1+r_{2}}, (35)

which map the AIAO and nematic tuning parameters r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} for r1,r2∈[0,∞)r_{1},r_{2}\in[0,\infty) onto the unit interval, α1,α2∈[0,1)\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in[0,1). The fixed-point equations for the eight parameters δ,e2,g12,α1,g22,λ,c,α2\delta,e^{2},g_{1}^{2},\alpha_{1},g_{2}^{2},\lambda,c,\alpha_{2} can be solved analytically in the limit N→∞N\to\infty. Starting from the large-NN solutions, we use a Newton-Raphson method in order to determine the fixed-point values and the corresponding scaling or critical exponents numerically at finite NN. For sufficiently large NN, we identify a unique interacting infrared stable fixed point, which we associate with the disordered LAB phase [15, 16, 17]. The corresponding fixed-point values for different values of NN, together with the associated scaling exponents, are given in Table 1. In addition, as expected from the mean-field analysis, we further find two quantum critical fixed points associated with nematic [26, 29] and AIAO [27, 30, 31] instabilities. Their corresponding fixed-point values and critical exponents are given in Tables 2 and 3, respectively.

As visible from Tables 1 and 2, the nematic fixed point and the LAB fixed point are located in the physical space of real couplings for N≥Nc=1.8555070​…N\geq N_{\text{c}}=1.8555070\dots (rounded to three decimal places for better readability in what follows). At N=NcN=N_{\text{c}}, the LAB fixed point collides with the nematic fixed point and for even lower numbers of quadratic band touching points N<NcN<N_{\text{c}}, the two fixed points take complex values with finite imaginary parts. This result is consistent with the earlier analyses [25, 28, 29]. For the LAB fixed point, we show the dynamical exponent zz, which is related to the fermion anomalous dimension as ηψ=2−z\eta_{\psi}=2-z, the photon anomalous dimension ηa\eta_{a}, the anomalous dimension ηϕ\eta_{\phi} of the AIAO order parameter field, the anomalous dimension ηφ\eta_{\varphi} of the nematic order parameter, as well as the two least negative eigenvalues of the stability matrix at the LAB fixed point, ω1\omega_{1} and ω2\omega_{2}, corresponding to leading and next-to-leading corrections to scaling. (We have labelled ω1\omega_{1} and ω2\omega_{2} such that ω1<ω2\omega_{1}<\omega_{2} at large NN, and smoothly connected to this limit for finite NN.) The scaling exponent ω1\omega_{1} reflects the fact that the anisotropy δ\delta becomes an exactly marginal operator in the limit of infinitely many quadratic band touching points N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. The scaling exponent ω2→0+\omega_{2}\rightarrow 0^{+} for N→Nc+N\rightarrow N_{\text{c}}^{+} signals the collision of the LAB fixed point with the nematic fixed point. For the nematic fixed point, we analogously show zz, ηa\eta_{a}, ηϕ\eta_{\phi}, and ηφ\eta_{\varphi}, as well as the inverse correlation-length exponent 1/ν1/\nu, corresponding to the unique positive eigenvalue of the stability matrix. We note that the AIAO order parameter is non-critical at the nematic quantum critical point, indicated by α1⋆=1\alpha_{1\star}=1. The corresponding anomalous dimension ηϕ\eta_{\phi} at the nematic fixed point determines the scaling of the AIAO correlation function only after subtracting the momentum-independent contribution. The fact that α2⋆∈(0,1)\alpha_{2\star}\in(0,1) at the nematic fixed point implies that the corresponding dimensionful mass parameter Λ2α2⋆/(1−α2⋆)\Lambda^{2}\alpha_{2\star}/(1-\alpha_{2\star}) vanishes in the infrared limit, consistent with the emergent scale invariance at criticality. The numerical values of zz, ηa\eta_{a}, ηφ\eta_{\varphi}, ω2\omega_{2}, and 1/ν1/\nu in Tables 1 and 2 precisely agree with the corresponding values given in Ref. [29]. This is a consequence of the fact that AIAO fluctuations are suppressed by the infinite mass of the AIAO order-parameter field ϕ\phi at the LAB and nematic fixed points, as indicated by the corresponding α1⋆=1\alpha_{1\star}=1.

As shown in Table 3, the AIAO fixed point exists for any number of quadratic band touching points N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and, therefore, is not involved in any fixed-point annihilations. The fixed point is characterized by maximal anisotropy δ⋆=−1\delta_{\star}=-1, which has the consequence that the location of the fixed point and the corresponding critical exponents can be computed analytically. In fact, as argued in C, the AIAO critical exponents are expected to be exact. Our results for zz, ηa\eta_{a}, ηϕ\eta_{\phi}, and 1/ν1/\nu also precisely agree with the earlier calculations [27, 31].

We have explicitly verified that locations and exponents of all three fixed points are independent from the parameters c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} introduced in Sec. 2.4.1. This implies that also our result for the critical number NcN_{\text{c}} at which the fixed-point collision takes place does depend on neither c1c_{1} nor c2c_{2}. This justifies a posteriori the earlier introduced restriction to an eight-dimensional theory space.

To summarize the fixed-point analysis, the flow equations in the dynamical bosonization scheme exhibit, at large NN, an infrared stable fixed point corresponding to the disordered LAB phase, along with two quantum critical fixed points associated with instabilities toward the AIAO antiferromagnetic Weyl semimetal and the nematic topological insulator, respectively. As NN is lowered toward a critical value Nc=1.856N_{\mathrm{c}}=1.856, the stable LAB fixed point and the quantum critical nematic fixed point approach each other and ultimately annihilate for N<NcN<N_{\mathrm{c}}. We now turn to the implications of this fixed-point annihilation for the phase diagram.

2.4.4 Phase diagram.

To obtain the zero-temperature phase diagram, Figs. 3(b)–(d), we numerically integrate out the flow equations for the eight parameters δ,e2,G1,α1,G2,λ,c,α2\delta,e^{2},G_{1},\alpha_{1},G_{2},\lambda,c,\alpha_{2} in d=3d=3 spatial dimensions, using varying initial effective interaction strengths in the AIAO (nematic) channel G1G_{1} (G2G_{2}), and fixed (δ,2​e2/(3​π2​Λ),α1,λ/2​π2​Λ,c​Λ2,α2)UV=(−12,1,110,−10585184,766,1425)\left(\delta,2e^{2}/(3\pi^{2}\Lambda),\alpha_{1},\lambda/\sqrt{2\pi^{2}\Lambda},c\Lambda^{2},\alpha_{2}\right)_{\text{UV}}=\left(-\frac{1}{2},1,\frac{1}{10},-\sqrt{\frac{105}{85184}},\frac{7}{66},\frac{14}{25}\right) at the ultraviolet scale. Here, G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} correspond to the four-fermion couplings in the original four-fermion action in Eq. (2), which are related to the Yukawa couplings g12g_{1}^{2} and g22g_{2}^{2} as

G1=g12r1andG2=g22r2,\displaystyle G_{1}=\frac{g_{1}^{2}}{r_{1}}\hskip 20.00003pt\text{and}\hskip 20.00003ptG_{2}=\frac{g_{2}^{2}}{r_{2}}, (36)

cf. Eq. (7). In order to allow for an easier comparison with the mean-field results and other studies, we have chosen to work with dimensionful quantities e2e^{2}, G1G_{1}, G2G_{2}, λ\lambda, and cc in this subsection. The initial values of the effective charge e2e^{2}, the cubic nematic self-interaction λ\lambda, the regularization parameter cc, and the nematic mass parameter α2\alpha_{2} have been chosen according to the location of the nematic fixed point in the limit of infinitely many quadratic band touching points N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. The factors of 2/(3​π2)2/(3\pi^{2}) and 1/2​π21/\sqrt{2\pi^{2}} in the definition of the starting values for e2e^{2} and λ\lambda arise from the coupling rescaling for δ=−1/2\delta=-1/2, as given after Eq. (31). While the location of the phase boundaries depends on the choice of the initial values, our universal results, such as the occurrence of a continuous order-to-order transition is independent of this choice. Depending on the chosen initial conditions, for N>NcN>N_{\text{c}}, we find a flow towards either of three different regimes: For small G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, the parameters flow towards the LAB fixed-point values. In particular, this implies that α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} remain positive at all RG scales. This regime is associated with the LAB phase. For positive G1G_{1} beyond a certain finite threshold, we find that α1\alpha_{1} becomes negative at some RG scale. Negative α1\alpha_{1} corresponds to a negative curvature of the effective potential in the AIAO sector. Consequently, we associate the flow of α1\alpha_{1} toward negative values with the onset of AIAO order. For positive G2G_{2} beyond a certain finite threshold, on the other hand, we find that α2\alpha_{2} becomes negative at some RG scale, which we associate with the onset of nematic order. In order to estimate the values of the order parameters in the two different ordered phases, we assume that the flow away from the quantum critical fixed point is dominated by simple dimensional scaling. This assumption only modifies nonuniversal properties of the observables; in particular, it does neither change the order of the transition nor the values of the corresponding critical exponents [40, 39, 41]. Under this assumption, the values of the order parameters can be computed from the RG time tIR=ln⁡bIRt_{\text{IR}}=\ln b_{\text{IR}}, at which the associated parameters α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}, respectively, turn negative. In particular, in the AIAO phase, the order parameter ⟨ϕ⟩\langle\phi\rangle is related to tIRt_{\text{IR}} via ⟨ϕ⟩∝exp⁡(−d+z−2+ηϕ2​tIR)=exp⁡(−2​tIR)\langle\phi\rangle\propto\exp(- \frac{d + z - 2 + \eta_\phi}{2} t_\text{IR})=\exp(- 2 t_\text{IR}), since z=2z=2 and ηϕ=1\eta_{\phi}=1 at the AIAO quantum critical fixed point for all numbers of quadratic band touching points N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and in d=3d=3 spatial dimensions. In the nematic phase, the corresponding order parameter ⟨φ⟩\langle\varphi\rangle can be computed analogously; however, one has to be careful which dynamical exponent and anomalous dimension to incorporate: For N=10N=10 quadratic band touching points, we identify ⟨φ⟩∝exp⁡(−d+z−2+ηφ2​tIR)=exp⁡(−2.072​tIR)\langle\varphi\rangle\propto\exp(- \frac{d + z - 2 + \eta_\varphi}{2} t_\text{IR})=\exp(- 2.072 t_\text{IR}), with z=1.971z=1.971 and ηφ=1.174\eta_{\varphi}=1.174 at the nematic fixed point, see Table 2. Likewise, for N=2N=2 quadratic band touching points, we employ again ⟨φ⟩∝exp⁡(−d+z−2+ηφ2​tIR)=exp⁡(−2.307​tIR)\langle\varphi\rangle\propto\exp(- \frac{d + z - 2 + \eta_\varphi}{2} t_\text{IR})=\exp(- 2.307 t_\text{IR}), since z=1.882z=1.882 and ηφ=1.732\eta_{\varphi}=1.732 at the nematic fixed point, see Table 2. However, for the case N=1N=1, and therewith after the fixed-point annihilation, we identify ⟨φ⟩∝exp⁡(−d+z−2+ηϕ2​tIR)=exp⁡(−2​tIR)\langle\varphi\rangle\propto\exp(- \frac{d + z - 2 + \eta_\phi}{2} t_\text{IR})=\exp(- 2 t_\text{IR}), with z=2z=2 and ηϕ=1\eta_{\phi}=1 from the annihilation-surviving AIAO fixed point, which governs the transition into the nematic phase.

The resulting quantum phase diagram for a representative value of N=10N=10 is shown in Fig. 3(b) and qualitatively aligns with the mean-field result in Fig. 3(a). As NN decreases, the LAB fixed point and the quantum critical fixed point associated with the nematic instability approach each other. This implies that the LAB phase shrinks in the phase diagram in favor of the nematic phase, as exemplified for N=2N=2 in Fig. 3(c). Upon further decreasing NN, the two fixed points eventually collide at a critical value Nc=1.856N_{\mathrm{c}}=1.856, in agreement with Ref. [29]. The fixed-point annihilation for N<NcN<N_{\mathrm{c}} alters the flow topology by removing the LAB phase. We emphasize that no additional fixed points are involved in the collision; in particular, the quantum critical fixed point associated with the AIAO instability remains within the physical space of real couplings for all N≥1N\geq 1. The resulting quantum phase diagram for the physical case of N=1N=1, relevant for the pyrochlore iridates, is shown in Fig. 3(d). Importantly, there is now a direct transition between the AIAO Weyl semimetal and the nematic topological insulator upon tuning a single parameter, G1G_{1}. Although the two ordered states break different symmetries, and the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm would predict a discontinuous transition, the presence of the quantum critical fixed point associated with the AIAO instability leads to a continuous transition without fine tuning, provided G2G_{2} is not too large.

To illustrate this fact, we show in Fig. 6(a) the nematic order parameter ⟨φ⟩∝⟨ψ†​γ5​ψ⟩\langle\varphi\rangle\propto\langle\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{5}\psi\rangle and the AIAO antiferromagnetic order parameter ⟨ϕ⟩∝⟨ψ†​γ45​ψ⟩\langle\phi\rangle\propto\langle\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{45}\psi\rangle for N=1N=1 as functions of the ultraviolet value of G1G_{1} while keeping the ultraviolet values of G2G_{2}, e2e^{2}, and δ\delta fixed. The two order parameters vanish continuously upon approaching the quantum critical point at G1cG_{\text{1c}} from above and below, respectively. The same behavior is observed for other values of G2G_{2}, e2e^{2}, and δ\delta, provided G2G_{2} is not too large. There is a direct continuous order-to-order quantum phase transition without an intermediate mixed phase and without additional fine tuning.

2.4.5 Asymmetry in energy scales.

A characteristic feature of the continuous order-to-order transition from fixed-point annihilation is a significant anisotropy in the effective energy scales on the two sides of the transition. In general, energy scales depend on microscopic parameters and therefore cannot be quantitatively predicted within our continuum model. However, at equal distances from criticality, we qualitatively find that the nematic order parameter for G1<G1cG_{1}<G_{\text{1c}} is typically several order of magnitude smaller than the AIAO order parameter for G1>G1cG_{1}>G_{\text{1c}}. This phenomenon arises as a direct consequence of the fixed-point annihilation occurring at Nc=1.856N_{\mathrm{c}}=1.856, which is only slightly above the physical value of N=1N=1. For NN just below NcN_{\mathrm{c}}, the complex LAB fixed point has a small imaginary part. As a result, the RG flow near the location in parameter space where the fixed-point annihilation has occurred becomes logarithmically slow. This slow flow leads to an exponential suppression of the effective energy scale associated with the nematic order, a phenomenon known as “walking behavior” in the field-theory literature [42, 43]. Walking behavior is observed in fixed-point annihilation scenarios across various systems, including quantum impurity models [44, 45, 46, 47], Potts models [48, 49, 50, 51], Abelian Higgs models [52, 53], Wess-Zumino-Witten models [54, 55, 56], QED3 [57, 58, 59, 60], and QCD4 [61, 62, 63, 64, 65].

To illustrate this point, we again assume that the flow away from the quantum critical fixed point is dominated by simple dimensional scaling. Up to prefactors of order one, we can then estimate the critical temperature on the AIAO side of the transition as TcAIAO∝exp⁡(−z​tIR)=exp⁡(−2​tIR)T_{\text{c}}^{\text{AIAO}}\propto\exp(- z t_\text{IR})=\exp(- 2 t_\text{IR}), where tIR=ln⁡bIRt_{\text{IR}}=\ln b_{\text{IR}} denotes the RG time at which the parameter α1\alpha_{1} turns negative. Similarly, on the nematic side of the transition, we can estimate the nematic critical temperature as Tcnem∝exp⁡(−2​tIR)T_{\text{c}}^{\text{nem}}\propto\exp(- 2 t_\text{IR}), with tIRt_{\text{IR}} denoting the RG time at which the parameter α2\alpha_{2} turns negative. For N=1N=1, the complex LAB fixed point is still reasonably close to the physical space of real couplings. This results in a regime with logarithmically slow flow and LAB-like behavior in a sizable finite-temperature regime [25, 29]. The corresponding crossover temperature T⋆LABT_{\star}^{\text{LAB}} between the nonuniversal high-temperature regime and the LAB-like regime at intermediate temperatures can be estimated via T⋆LAB∝exp⁡(−2​tLAB)T_{\star}^{\text{LAB}}\propto\exp(- 2 t_\text{LAB}), where tLABt_{\text{LAB}} corresponds to the RG time at which the flow enters the slow-flow regime associated with the complex LAB fixed point. A natural way to estimate tLABt_{\text{LAB}} is to analyze the dimensionless vector of flow parameters r→​(t)≔(δ,e2/[2​π2​(1−δ2)​Λ],G1​Λ/[2​π2​(1−δ2)],α1,G2​Λ/(2​π2),λ/2​π2​Λ,c​Λ2,α2)​(t)\vec{r}(t)\coloneqq(\delta,e^{2}/[2\pi^{2}(1-\delta^{2})\Lambda],G_{1}\Lambda/[2\pi^{2}(1-\delta^{2})],\alpha_{1},G_{2}\Lambda/(2\pi^{2}),\lambda/\sqrt{2\pi^{2}\Lambda},c\Lambda^{2},\alpha_{2})(t) as function of RG time tt. Figure 7(a) shows the corresponding flow speed ‖ⅆr→​(t)ⅆt‖\norm{\frac{\rmd\vec{r} (t)}{\rmd t}} as function of t∈[0,tIR]t\in[0,t_{\text{IR}}]. We observe two regimes in which the flow becomes slow. Comparing the flow parameters r→​(t)\vec{r}(t) with the values of the different fixed points, we identify the first (second) regime of slow flow to arise from the vicinity to the AIAO (complex LAB) fixed point. The first minimum in ‖ⅆr→​(t)ⅆt‖\norm{\frac{\rmd\vec{r} (t)}{\rmd t}} thus corresponds to the quantum critical regime, while the second minimum corresponds to the LAB regime. The local maximum in ‖ⅆr→​(t)ⅆt‖\norm{\frac{\rmd\vec{r} (t)}{\rmd t}} in between the two minima at intermediate time tLABt_{\text{LAB}} thus corresponds to the crossover between the two regimes.

In sum, on the nematic side of the transition, we find a sizable intermediate-temperature regime between the critical temperature TcnemT_{\mathrm{c}}^{\text{nem}} and the crossover temperature T⋆LABT_{\star}^{\text{LAB}}. On the AIAO side, there is only a single minimum in the flow speed ‖ⅆr→​(t)ⅆt‖\norm{\frac{\rmd\vec{r} (t)}{\rmd t}}, associated with the quantum critical regime, indicating the absence of an additional intermediate-temperature regime. The resulting finite-temperature phase diagram is shown in Fig. 6(b), and illustrates the advertised asymmetry in the effective energy scales on the two different sides of the continuous order-to-order transition. On the nematic side of the transition, the critical temperature is significantly suppressed by several orders of magnitude in comparison with the AIAO side. This suppression of the nematic order creates a broad intermediate regime at finite temperature, separated from the nonuniversal high-energy regime by a crossover scale T⋆LABT_{\star}^{\text{LAB}}. In this regime, the RG flow is “stuck” in the vicinity of the, now imaginary, LAB fixed point [25, 29], and thermodynamic and transport observables exhibit power laws with nontrivial exponents, characteristic of a non-Fermi liquid [17]. While the asymmetry in the effective energy scales on either side of the transition decreases with increasing G2G_{2}, we find it to remain significant for all parameter sets that we have studied. This indicates that it can serve as a distinctive signature for experimentally identifying the proposed mechanism for continuous order-to-order transitions from fixed-point annihilation.

In the present example, the proximity of the physical value N=1N=1 to the critical value Nc=1.856N_{\mathrm{c}}=1.856 results in an asymmetry large enough to potentially hinder direct experimental verification. However, since the asymmetry diminishes with increasing distance from the quantum critical point, finite nematic order may still be observable, provided the system is sufficiently removed from the critical region, leading to indirect evidence of the proposed continuous order-to-order transition. Another possible indirect signature of the mechanism is the appearance of “drifting” exponents in the pseudo-critical regime above the nematic phase, resulting from the fixed-point annihilation [25, 29].

2.4.6 Universality class.

The quantum critical behavior of the continuous order-to-order transition is governed by the RG flow near the fixed point associated with the AIAO instability. In the present model, this fixed point is situated at extreme cubic anisotropy [27, 31], allowing for the exact computation of all critical exponents, see C. We find that the anomalous dimensions for both the AIAO and nematic orders, respectively are ηϕ=ηφ=1\eta_{\phi}=\eta_{\varphi}=1, the correlation-length exponents νϕ=νφ=1\nu_{\phi}=\nu_{\varphi}=1, and the dynamical exponent z=2z=2. Assuming hyperscaling holds, we find that the two order parameters scale as ⟨ϕ⟩∝(G1−G1c)βϕ\langle\phi\rangle\propto(G_{1}-G_{\text{1c}})^{\beta_{\phi}} and ⟨φ⟩∝(G1c−G1)βφ\langle\varphi\rangle\propto(G_{\text{1c}}-G_{1})^{\beta_{\varphi}} as G1G_{1} approaches G1cG_{\text{1c}} from above and below, respectively, with the same exponent βϕ=βφ=2\beta_{\phi}=\beta_{\varphi}=2.

This theoretical expectation can be explicitly confirmed within our numerical analysis. To this end, we replot the data from Fig. 6 using a double-logarithmic scale. Figure 7(b) displays the AIAO order parameter as a function of the tuning parameter G1−G1​cG_{1}-G_{1\text{c}} on the AIAO side of the transition. Near the critical point, the values obtained from numerical integration (solid line) approach the expected behavior with slope βϕ=2\beta_{\phi}=2 (dashed line), as expected from the fixed-point analysis. Similarly, Fig. 7(c) displays the nematic order parameter as a function of G1​c−G1G_{1\text{c}}-G_{1} on the nematic side of the transition. While corrections to scaling appear to be more significant in this case, the leading behavior is still consistent with the expected slope βφ=2\beta_{\varphi}=2. We attribute the sizable scaling corrections to the slow flow arising from the fixed-point annihilation and the marginal anisotropy parameter δ\delta, which leads to quasiuniversal behavior over several length scales [31]. Lastly, Fig. 7(d) depicts the crossover temperature T⋆LABT_{\star}^{\text{LAB}} as a function of G1​c−G1G_{1\text{c}}-G_{1} on the nematic side of the transition. Again, the numerical result (solid line) in the vicinity of the critical point is consistent with the expectation from the fixed-point analysis (dashed line), namely T⋆LAB∝(G1​c−G1)ν​zT_{\star}^{\text{LAB}}\propto(G_{1\text{c}}-G_{1})^{\nu z} with ν​z=2\nu z=2.

Let us end this section with two general comments on the universality class of an order-to-order quantum phase transition caused by the proposed fixed-point annihilation mechanism. First, it is of course no coincidence that the two correlation-length exponents νϕ\nu_{\phi} and νφ\nu_{\varphi} associated with the AIAO and nematic correlation functions align in our theory, ν=νϕ=νφ\nu=\nu_{\phi}=\nu_{\varphi}. This has to hold for any order-to-order quantum phase transition arising from fixed-point annihilation as a consequence of the presence of a single divergent length scale at the annihilation-surviving quantum critical fixed point. Second, all other pairs of critical exponents associated with the two different order parameters may in general take on different values. The fact that this does not happen in the present case can be understood as a consequence of the maximal anisotropy δ⋆=−1\delta_{\star}=-1 at the AIAO fixed point, leading to ηϕ=ηφ=1\eta_{\phi}=\eta_{\varphi}=1, which, together with the hyperscaling assumption, implies that all pairs of exponents agree.

3 Kagome quantum magnets

3.1 Model

Although the proposed mechanism for a continuous order-to-order transition does not depend on the formation of fractionalized quasiparticles, it is possible to emerge also in conjunction with fractionalization phenomena. To illustrate this point, consider the extended Heisenberg model on the kagome lattice, defined by the Hamiltonian

ℋ=J1​∑⟨i​j⟩S→i⋅S→j+J2​∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩S→i⋅S→j+J3​∑⟨⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩⟩S→i⋅S→j.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\!\langle ij\rangle\!\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}+J_{3}\sum_{\langle\!\langle\!\langle ij\rangle\!\rangle\!\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}. (37)

Here, S→i\vec{S}_{i} represents a spin-1/21/2 at site ii, while ⟨i​j⟩{\langle ij\rangle}, ⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩{\langle\!\langle ij\rangle\!\rangle}, and ⟨⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩⟩{\langle\!\langle\!\langle ij\rangle\!\rangle\!\rangle} correspond to first-, second-, and third-neighbor bonds, respectively, with J1J_{1}, J2J_{2}, and J3J_{3} denoting the associated exchange couplings, see Fig. 9(a). The model describes magnetic Mott insulators crystallizing in a layered kagome structure, such as herbertsmithite ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2 [66], kapellasite Cu3Zn(OH)6Cl2 [67], or YCu3(OH)6.5Br2.5 [68, 69]. For dominant antiferromagnetic J1>0J_{1}>0, numerical simulations at finite temperature or on finite lattices observe no evidence for any long-range-ordered state, suggesting the formation of a quantum spin liquid [70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78]. The nature of this state has been a matter of significant debate, with recent simulations indicating a gapless U(1) Dirac spin liquid [74, 75, 76]. For increasing second- and third-neighbor interactions J2J_{2} and J3J_{3}, a transition to a gapped chiral spin liquid, characterized by broken time reversal symmetry with finite scalar spin chirality ⟨S→i⋅(S→j×S→k)⟩\langle\vec{S}_{i}\cdot(\vec{S}_{j}\times\vec{S}_{k})\rangle, has been found [79, 80, 81, 82, 83]. For instance, fixing the second- and third-nearest-neighbor couplings as J2/J1=J3/J1=αJ_{2}/J_{1}=J_{3}/J_{1}=\alpha with antiferromagnetic next-neighbor coupling J1>0J_{1}>0, the transition occurs at αc≃0.4\alpha_{\mathrm{c}}\simeq 0.4 [79]. The transition has been argued to be continuous [79] and described by the QED3-Gross-Neveu model with N=2N=2 four-component Dirac fields [74, 84, 85, 86, 87, 88, 89]. The QED3-Gross-Neveu model describes fermionic excitations ψ\psi and ψ†\psi^{\dagger} arising from fractionalization of the spin degrees of freedom, interacting via an emergent U(1) gauge field aμa_{\mu} and additional local four-fermion interactions,

SQED3-GN\displaystyle S_{\text{QED${}_{3}$-GN}} =∫d3x[ψ¯iγμ(∂μ−ⅈ​eNaμ)ψi+14fμ​ν2\displaystyle=\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential[3]{x}\Bigg[\bar{\psi}_{i}\gamma_{\mu}\left(\partial_{\mu}-\frac{\rmi e}{\sqrt{N}}a_{\mu}\right)\psi_{i}+\frac{1}{4}f_{\mu\nu}^{2}
−G12​N(ψ¯iγ45ψi)2−G22​N(ψ¯iγμψi)2].\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt-\frac{G_{1}}{2N}\left(\bar{\psi}_{i}\gamma_{45}\psi_{i}\right)^{2}-\frac{G_{2}}{2N}\left(\bar{\psi}_{i}\gamma_{\mu}\psi_{i}\right)^{2}\Biggr]\,. (38)

Here, ψi\psi_{i} and ψ¯i≔ψ†​γ3\bar{\psi}_{i}\coloneqq\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{3} denote N=2N=2 flavors of four-component Dirac spinors in (2+1)(2+1)-dimensional Euclidean space-time, fμ​ν=∂μaν−∂νaμf_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}a_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}a_{\mu} is the U(1) field-strength tensor associated with the U(1) gauge field aμa_{\mu}, the 4×44\times 4 matrices γμ\gamma_{\mu} satisfy the Clifford algebra, and γ45≔ⅈ​γ4​γ5\gamma_{45}\coloneqq\rmi\gamma_{4}\gamma_{5} is the Hermitian product of the two chiral gamma matrices in the reducible four-component spinor representation. For notational simplicity, we have assumed the summation convention over repeated flavor indices i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N and space-time indices μ=1,2,3\mu=1,2,3. Among others, the model features ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} time reversal and SU(2​N2N) flavor symmetry.

3.2 RG analysis

In 2+1 dimensions, the gauge coupling e2e^{2} has positive mass dimension and flows to a finite value in the infrared. The four-fermion couplings G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are power-counting irrelevant, but can be generated by the finite gauge coupling. On the level of mean-field theory, the coupling G1G_{1}, if tuned beyond a certain finite threshold, induces a transition between the Dirac spin liquid for G1<G1​cG_{1}<G_{1\text{c}} and the chiral spin liquid for G1>G1​cG_{1}>G_{1\text{c}}. The latter is characterized by a finite vacuum expectation value of the fermion bilinear ⟨ψ¯i​γ45​ψi⟩≠0\langle\bar{\psi}_{i}\gamma_{45}\psi_{i}\rangle\neq 0, which breaks time reversal symmetry [90]. The four-fermion coupling G1G_{1} can thus be understood to parameterize the second- and third-nearest-neighbor interactions J2=J3J_{2}=J_{3} in the microscopic model. The coupling G2G_{2} is generated by the RG flow and is therefore included from the outset. Indeed, treating G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} on equal footing is essential for identifying the continuous order-to-order transition.

At one-loop order, the flow equations for the QED3-Gross-Neveu model read [58, 85]

ⅆe2ⅆln⁡b\displaystyle\frac{\rmd e^{2}}{\rmd\ln b} =(1−ηa)​e2,\displaystyle=\left(1-\eta_{a}\right)e^{2}, (39)
ⅆG1ⅆln⁡b\displaystyle\frac{\rmd G_{1}}{\rmd\ln b} =−G1+163​N​e2​G1+8N​e2​G2−4N​e4+2​(2​N−1)N​G12\displaystyle=-G_{1}+\frac{16}{3N}e^{2}G_{1}+\frac{8}{N}e^{2}G_{2}-\frac{4}{N}e^{4}+\frac{2(2N-1)}{N}G_{1}^{2}
−4N​G22−6N​G1​G2,\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt-\frac{4}{N}G_{2}^{2}-\frac{6}{N}G_{1}G_{2}, (40)
ⅆG2ⅆln⁡b\displaystyle\frac{\rmd G_{2}}{\rmd\ln b} =−G2+83​N​e2​G1−2​(2​N+1)3​N​G22−2N​G1​G2,\displaystyle=-G_{2}+\frac{8}{3N}e^{2}G_{1}-\frac{2(2N+1)}{3N}G_{2}^{2}-\frac{2}{N}G_{1}G_{2}, (41)

with gauge field anomalous dimension ηa=43​e2\eta_{a}=\frac{4}{3}e^{2}. Above, we employed the rescaling e2↦2​π2​Λ​e2e^{2}\mapsto 2\pi^{2}\Lambda e^{2}, G1↦2​π2​Λ−1​G1G_{1}\mapsto 2\pi^{2}\Lambda^{-1}G_{1}, and G2↦2​π2​Λ−1​G2G_{2}\mapsto 2\pi^{2}\Lambda^{-1}G_{2}, where Λ\Lambda denotes the ultraviolet cutoff. Figure 8(a) illustrates the fixed-point structure of the model. For sufficiently large NN, the infrared attractive plane e2=e⋆2=3/4e^{2}=e^{2}_{\star}=3/4 hosts a fully infrared stable fixed point (cQED3), associated with the conformal phase of QED3 [57, 91, 58, 59]. In the context of the extended Heisenberg spin-1/2 model on the kagome lattice, the latter can be understood as a U(1) Dirac spin liquid [74, 75, 76]. In addition, the plane features two quantum critical fixed points, associated with instabilities towards Ising ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} time reversal symmetry breaking (QCPIsing{}_{\text{Ising}}) and SU(2​N2N) flavor symmetry breaking (QCPflavor{}_{\text{flavor}}) ground states, respectively [57, 59]. On the kagome lattice, the former can be understood as chiral spin liquid [74, 84], while the latter is expected to realize valence bond solid order [92].

For decreasing NN, the infrared stable cQED3 fixed point and the quantum critical QCPflavor{}_{\text{flavor}} fixed point approach each other and eventually collide at a critical flavor number NcN_{\text{c}}. This is illustrated in Figs. 8(b)–(d), which shows the RG flow in the G1G_{1}-G2G_{2} plane for fixed e2=e⋆2e^{2}=e^{2}_{\star} and different values of NN above, at, and below the critical flavor number NcN_{\text{c}}. For N<NcN<N_{\text{c}}, the cQED3 and QCPflavor{}_{\text{flavor}} fixed points are located in the complex plane, leaving behind a runaway flow in the space of real couplings. Importantly, the fixed point QCPIsing{}_{\text{Ising}}, associated with the time-reversal-symmetry-breaking instability, remains unaffected by the collision and annihilation process. For N<NcN<N_{\text{c}}, it distinguishes between two different regimes characterized by runaway flows: Consider the line of starting values given by e2=e⋆2e^{2}=e^{2}_{\star} and G2=0G_{2}=0 at the ultraviolet scale. For G1>G1⋆G_{1}>G_{1\star}, the flow diverges towards (G1,G2)→(∞,0)(G_{1},G_{2})\to(\infty,0) at a finite RG scale, indicating spontaneous time reversal symmetry breaking. For G1<G1⋆G_{1}<G_{1\star}, on the other hand, the flow diverges towards (G1,G2)→(−∞,−∞)(G_{1},G_{2})\to(-\infty,-\infty), which has previously been interpreted as an instability towards flavor symmetry breaking [90, 85, 59]. This suggests that QCPIsing{}_{\text{Ising}} governs for N<NcN<N_{\text{c}} a continuous quantum phase transition on the between two long-range ordered states that break different symmetries. At the one-loop order, we find the critical flavor number as Nc=6.24N_{\text{c}}=6.24. Higher-loop contributions may reduce the number, but most analytical estimates [57, 91, 59, 93, 94] appear to suggest that the fixed-point collision and annihilation occurs above the physical number N=2N=2 relevant for the kagome quantum magnets. (We emphasize, however, that we are not aware of clear numerical evidence for the scenario in an unbiased simulation of the QED3-Gross-Neveu model, such as Monte Carlo [95, 96].) If indeed Nc>2N_{\text{c}}>2 in the QED3-Gross-Neveu model, it implies for the extended Heisenberg spin-1/2 model on the kagome lattice that (1) the U(1) Dirac spin liquid becomes unstable at the lowest temperatures towards a valence bond solid ordered ground state and (2) the quantum phase transition between the valence bond solid, stabilized for α<0.4\alpha<0.4, and the chiral spin liquid, stabilized for α>0.4\alpha>0.4, is continuous and governed by the QCPIsing{}_{\text{Ising}} fixed point. The resulting schematic phase diagram is depicted in Fig. 9(b). An explicit computation of the order parameters across the order-to-order transition would require introducing the corresponding Hubbard-Stratonovich fields within the dynamical bosonization framework of Sec. 2, which we leave for future work.

4 Conclusions

We have proposed a mechanism for generic continuous order-to-order quantum phase transitions that operates independently of fractionalization. This mechanism is based on the collision and annihilation of two RG fixed points, and may be realized in pyrochlore iridates and kagome quantum magnets. Further possible realizations in quantum impurity models and quantum chromodynamics with additional four-fermion interactions are discussed in D. A distinctive experimental or numerical signature of the mechanism is a pronounced asymmetry in the effective energy scales between the two sides of the transition, characterized by a significantly lower critical temperature and a much smaller order parameter on the side where the order emerges from fixed-point annihilation.

The fixed-point annihilation mechanism responsible for the continuous order-to-order transition, discussed in this work, should be contrasted with previously discussed scenarios, where fixed-point annihilation gives rise to weak first-order transitions [52, 60, 43, 56]. Such a scenario has recently been discussed in the context of SU(NN) quantum spin models on two-dimensional lattices, which are believed to be described by the NN-component Abelian Higgs model [97, 5, 53, 3, 11]. Similar scenarios have also been discussed in QQ-state Potts models [48, 49, 50, 51] and tensor O(N)(N) models [98, 99, 100, 101]. In all these examples, a critical fixed point collides with a bicritical fixed point, and both disappear into the complex plane as a function of some external parameter. In these systems, after the fixed-point collision, a continuous order-to-order transition is therefore not possible without additional fine tuning. In the examples discussed in the present work, by contrast, a critical fixed point collides with an infrared stable fixed point, destabilizing the symmetric phase and leaving behind a continuous transition between two different orders.

Appendix B Fermionic RG flow

In this appendix, we show that the dynamically bosonized flow equations of our model using Hubbard-Stratonovich fields ϕ\phi and φ\varphi, as obtained in Sec. 2.4, reduce, in the limit of infinite order-parameter masses, α1,α2→1\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\to 1, to those of a purely fermionic model, obtained without introducing order-parameter fields explicitly. The latter is defined by the action

SF\displaystyle S_{\text{F}} =∫dτd3x→{ψ†(∂τ+∑a=15(1+saδ)daγa+ⅈ​eNa)ψ\displaystyle=\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential{\tau}\differential[3]{\vec x}\Biggl\{\psi^{\dagger}\left(\partial_{\tau}+\sum_{a=1}^{5}(1+s_{a}\delta)d_{a}\gamma_{a}+\frac{\rmi e}{\sqrt{N}}a\right)\psi
+12(∇a)2−G12​N(ψ†γ45ψ)2−G22​N∑a=15(ψ†γaψ)2},\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt+\frac{1}{2}(\nabla a)^{2}-\frac{G_{1}}{2N}(\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{45}\psi)^{2}-\frac{G_{2}}{2N}\sum_{a=1}^{5}(\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_{a}\psi)^{2}\Biggr\}\,, (63)

and has been studied previously in Refs. [25, 29, 30]. The goal of the comparison is twofold. First, we want to demonstrate that our calculations are consistent with the fermionic ones presented in Refs. [25, 29, 30]. Second, we want build some intuition on fermionic flows with respect to the proposed fixed-point annihilation mechanism, which prepares us for the examples discussed below. We note, however, that the limit of infinite order-parameter masses is in principle insufficient to compute order parameters in symmetry-broken phases, as required for explicitly demonstrating the proposed order-to-order transition. This is because fermionic RG flows diverge in the case of spontaneous symmetry breaking.

We start from the flow equations in the dynamical bosonization scheme in terms of the couplings δ\delta, e2e^{2}, G1G_{1}, α1\alpha_{1}, G2G_{2}, λ\lambda, cc, and α2\alpha_{2}. In the limit of infinite order-parameter masses, α1,α2→1\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\to 1, the flow equations for δ\delta, e2e^{2}, G1G_{1}, and G2G_{2} become independent of λ\lambda and cc.
