To arrive at the above flow equations, we have rescaled the AIAO order-parameter mass in the dynamically bosonized flow equations as r1↦(1−δ2)​r1r_{1}\mapsto(1-\delta^{2})r_{1}, such that G1=g12/r1G_{1}=g_{1}^{2}/r_{1} remains finite at the AIAO quantum critical point. The dimensionless couplings occurring in Eqs. (64)–(69) are then related to the dimensionful couplings of the microscopic action, Eq. (63), via the rescaling e2↦2​π2​Λ4−d​(1−δ2)​e2e^{2}\mapsto 2\pi^{2}\Lambda^{4-d}(1-\delta^{2})e^{2}, G1↦2​π2​Λ2−d​G1G_{1}\mapsto 2\pi^{2}\Lambda^{2-d}G_{1}, and G2↦2​π2​Λ2−d​G2G_{2}\mapsto 2\pi^{2}\Lambda^{2-d}G_{2}. For N=1N=1, the flow equations for the anisotropy δ\delta, the charge e2e^{2}, and the anomalous dimensions ηψ\eta_{\psi} and ηa\eta_{a} agree with the previous calculation [30]. For all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, but δ=0\delta=0, the flow equations for the charge e2e^{2} and the anomalous dimensions ηψ\eta_{\psi} and ηa\eta_{a} agree with those of Refs. [25, 29]. The flow of G2G_{2} also agrees, with the exception of slight differences in the prefactors of the terms ∝G1​G2\propto G_{1}G_{2} and ∝G12\propto G_{1}^{2}. These can be attributed to the fact that we have performed the dynamical bosonization scheme only in the nematic channel, leading to a Fierz-incomplete calculation. This also explains the (minor) differences in the flow of G1G_{1} in comparison with the corresponding calculation in Refs. [25, 29].

For N>1.91N>1.91, the fermionic flow equations feature a fully infrared stable fixed point, associated with the LAB phase, as well as two quantum critical fixed points, associated with the instabilities towards nematic and AIAO orders, respectively. We note that the AIAO fixed point in the point-like limit, in contrast to our results in the dynamical bosonization scheme (Sec. 2.4.3), exhibits an additional marginally relevant direction, associated with the flow of the anisotropy parameter δ\delta. This is a known artifact of the fermionic RG flow that can be attributed to the negligence of AIAO order-parameter fluctuations in the point-like limit [31]. For N=1.91N=1.91, the infrared stable LAB fixed point and the nematic quantum critical point collide and subsequently disappear into the complex plane for N<1.91N<1.91, in qualitative agreement with the fixed-point structure obtained from the dynamically bosonized RG flow, discussed in Sec. 2.4, as well as the earlier works [25, 29, 30]. In agreement with the dynamically bosonized RG flow, the fixed-point collision takes place in the isotropic G1G_{1}-G2G_{2} plane defined by δ=0\delta=0 and finite effective charge e2=15​N4+15​Ne^{2}=\frac{15N}{4+15N}. The flow in this plane is depicted for different values of NN in Fig. 11 (top row), illustrating the fixed-point collision. Although all fixed points in this section are analytically accessible, we refrain from stating their expressions here, as they are rather lengthy.

Importantly, the AIAO fixed point does not take part in the collision and annihilation of the LAB fixed point with the nematic fixed point, but remains in the physical space of real couplings for all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, in agreement with our results in the dynamical bosonization scheme. The AIAO fixed point is located in the plane defined by anisotropy δ=−1\delta=-1 and effective charge e2=916e^{2}=\frac{9}{16}. The flow in this plane is depicted for different values of NN in Fig. 11 (bottom row), illustrating the fact that the AIAO fixed point persists for all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}. We conclude, that, at least in the case of Luttinger semimetals, the presented fixed-point annihilation mechanism is also available in the purely fermionic formulation.

Appendix C Higher-loop corrections

In this appendix, we demonstrate that the critical exponents at the AIAO fixed point we have found at the one-loop order do not receive higher-loop corrections, and are thus expected to be exact. This is ultimately another consequence of the maximal anisotropy δ⋆=−1\delta_{\star}=-1 at the AIAO fixed point. Our argument is independent of the number of quadratic band touching points NN and therefore holds for all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}.

As argued in Ref. [31] for G2=0G_{2}=0, higher-loop corrections in the AIAO and charge sector are fully suppressed at the AIAO fixed point. This can be understood as a consequence of the fact that the AIAO fixed point is located at maximal anisotropy δ⋆=−1\delta_{\star}=-1. Here, it can be seen from the fact that the fixed point values for e2e^{2} and g12g_{1}^{2} are finite after performing the anisotropy-dependent reparametrization (e2,g12)↦(1−δ2)​(e2,g12)(e^{2},g_{1}^{2})\mapsto(1-\delta^{2})(e^{2},g_{1}^{2}), cf. Sec. 2.4. After this rescaling, every higher-loop diagram now comes with a strictly positive power of (1−δ2)(1-\delta^{2}). As a result, all higher-loop corrections are strongly suppressed in the vicinity of the AIAO fixed point at anisotropy δ⋆=−1\delta_{\star}=-1, rendering the one-loop flow equations asymptotically exact, see Ref. [31] for details and Refs. [103, 104] for a different model with analogous behavior.

In our extended model for finite G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, the AIAO fixed point remains to be located at maximal anisotropy δ⋆=−1\delta_{\star}=-1 and additionally lies now at infinite nematic boson mass r2⋆→∞r_{2\star}\to\infty, cf. Table 3. These two fixed-point values suppress all higher-loop diagrams contributing to the flow equations relevant for the critical exponents. For instance, all higher-loop corrections to the flow of the anisotropy δ\delta, to the effective charge e2e^{2}, and to the AIAO Yukawa coupling g12g_{1}^{2} are either strongly suppressed by strictly positive powers of (1−δ2)(1-\delta^{2}) (these are the already known contributions arising in the theory for G1=0G_{1}=0) and/or by strictly positive powers of 1/(1+r2)1/(1+r_{2}) (these are new contributions with at least one internal nematic boson) in the vicinity of the AIAO fixed point. Consequently, the anomalous dimension of the fermion ηψ=0\eta_{\psi}=0, the dynamical exponent z=2−ηψ=2z=2-\eta_{\psi}=2, the anomalous dimension of the photon ηa=4−d\eta_{a}=4-d, and the anomalous dimension the AIAO boson ηϕ=4−d\eta_{\phi}=4-d are exact critical exponents of the AIAO fixed point. A similar argument can be made for the new flow equation of the nematic Yukawa coupling g22g_{2}^{2} here, since all loop-correction fall again into two distinct classes, as depicted in Fig. 12, which both vanish at the AIAO fixed point. The first class of diagrams consists of all loop-corrections involving at least one internal nematic boson. Since internal nematic bosons give rise to the appearance of strictly positive powers of 1/(1+r2)1/(1+r_{2}), the whole first class of diagrams is suppressed in the vicinity of the AIAO fixed point located at infinite nematic mass r2⋆=∞r_{2\star}=\infty. Any higher-loop order correction that is not of the above form involves only internal fermion, photon, and/or AIAO boson propagators and is, following the argument presented in Ref. [31], expected to be suppressed by a strictly positive power of (1−δ2)(1-\delta^{2}). Therefore, also the anomalous dimension of the nematic order parameter field ηφ=4−d\eta_{\varphi}=4-d is expected to be exact at the AIAO fixed point. The only exponent left to think about is the correlation-length exponent ν\nu. Note that the AIAO and nematic propagator display the same exponent ν=νϕ=νφ\nu=\nu_{\phi}=\nu_{\varphi}, since there is only one divergent length scale present at the AIAO fixed point, as demonstrated in the previous section. Analogously to the flow equation of the anisotropy δ\delta, the effective charge e2e^{2}, and the AIAO Yukawa coupling g12g_{1}^{2}, higher-loop corrections to the flow of the AIAO mass r1r_{1} are either strongly suppressed by strictly positive powers of (1−δ2)(1-\delta^{2}) and/or by strictly positive powers of 1/(1+r2)1/(1+r_{2}) in the vicinity of the AIAO fixed point. As a consequence, the stability matrix is of block triangular form with 1/ν=2−ηϕ=d−21/\nu=2-\eta_{\phi}=d-2 as the only (strictly) positive eigenvalue.

Appendix D Further examples of continuous order-to-order transitions

In this appendix, we provide two further examples for continuous order-to-order transitions arising from fixed-point annihilation in interacting many-body systems.

D.1 Anisotropic spin-boson model

As an example for a model featuring a continuous order-to-order transition from fixed-point annihilation that is directly amenable to large-scale numerical simulations, consider the anisotropic spin-boson model, which describes a single spin S→\vec{S} in a fluctuating magnetic field h→\vec{h} with an XXZ anisotropy, defined by the Hamiltonian [105]

ℋspin-boson=gx​y​(hx​Sx+hy​Sy)+gz​hz​Sz+ℋbulk​(h→).\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\text{spin-boson}}=g_{xy}(h^{x}S^{x}+h^{y}S^{y})+g_{z}h^{z}S^{z}+\mathcal{H}_{\text{bulk}}(\vec{h}). (70)

Here, gx​yg_{xy} and gzg_{z} correspond to in-plane and out-of-plane components of the gg tensor, respectively, and the bulk Hamiltonian ℋbulk​(h→)\mathcal{H}_{\text{bulk}}(\vec{h}) is chosen such that the fluctuations of the magnetic field are Gaussian, with power-law correlation

⟨𝒯τ​ha​(τ)​hb​(0)⟩∝δa​b|τ|2−ϵ,\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{T}_{\tau}h^{a}(\tau)h^{b}(0)\rangle\propto\frac{\delta^{ab}}{|\tau|^{2-\epsilon}}, (71)

where 𝒯τ\mathcal{T}_{\tau} corresponds to the time ordering operator in imaginary time τ\tau. The bath exponent ϵ\epsilon represents an external tuning parameter, and we consider the case of small positive ϵ∈(0,1/2)\epsilon\in(0,1/2). The above spin-boson model may be realized as an effective description of a quantum impurity in a two-dimensional antiferromagnet in the vicinity of a quantum critical point [106, 107, 108].

The RG flow equations for the two couplings gx​yg_{xy} and gzg_{z} up to two-loop order read [109, 110]

ⅆgx​y2ⅆln⁡b\displaystyle\frac{\rmd g^{2}_{xy}}{\rmd\ln b} =ϵ​gx​y2−gx​y2​(gx​y2+gz2)+gx​y4​(gx​y2+gz2),\displaystyle=\epsilon g^{2}_{xy}-g^{2}_{xy}(g^{2}_{xy}+g^{2}_{z})+g_{xy}^{4}(g^{2}_{xy}+g^{2}_{z}), (72)
ⅆgz2ⅆln⁡b\displaystyle\frac{\rmd g^{2}_{z}}{\rmd\ln b} =ϵ​gz2−2​gx​y2​gz2+2​gx​y2​gz4,\displaystyle=\epsilon g^{2}_{z}-2g^{2}_{xy}g^{2}_{z}+2g^{2}_{xy}g_{z}^{4}, (73)

where we have rescaled gx​y2↦Λϵ​gx​y2g^{2}_{xy}\mapsto\Lambda^{\epsilon}g^{2}_{xy} and gz2↦Λϵ​gz2g_{z}^{2}\mapsto\Lambda^{\epsilon}g_{z}^{2}. The flow is illustrated for different values of 0<ϵ<1/20<\epsilon<1/2 in Fig. 13. For ϵ>0\epsilon>0, both couplings gx​y2g_{xy}^{2} and gz2g_{z}^{2} are infrared relevant. For gx​y2<gz2g_{xy}^{2}<g_{z}^{2} at the ultraviolet scale, the parameters flow towards (gx​y2,gz2)→(0,+∞)(g_{xy}^{2},g_{z}^{2})\to(0,+\infty). This regime is associated with an Ising ordered phase, in which the spin forms local order with a finite moment along the zz direction. The zz-localized phase spontaneously breaks Ising ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry [47]. For gx​y2>gz2g_{xy}^{2}>g_{z}^{2} at the ultraviolet scale, the phase structure depends on the value of the external tuning parameter ϵ\epsilon. This is due to a fixed-point annihilation that takes place at a critical value of the tuning parameter ϵc=1/4\epsilon_{\mathrm{c}}=1/4. For ϵ<ϵc=1/4\epsilon<\epsilon_{\mathrm{c}}=1/4 and gx​y2g_{xy}^{2} above, but not too far from gz2g_{z}^{2}, the flow is attracted by a fully infrared stable fixed point, corresponding to an interacting disordered phase (D). For large gx​y2g_{xy}^{2}, the parameters flow towards (gx​y2,gz2)→(+∞,0)(g_{xy}^{2},g_{z}^{2})\to(+\infty,0). This regime is associated with an XY ordered phase, in which the spin forms local order with a finite moment perpendicular to the zz direction. For ϵ=ϵc\epsilon=\epsilon_{\mathrm{c}}, the fixed point D collides with the quantum critical fixed point associated with the onset of XY order. Now for ϵ>ϵc\epsilon>\epsilon_{\mathrm{c}}, the parameters flow towards (gx​y2,gz2)→(+∞,0)(g_{xy}^{2},g_{z}^{2})\to(+\infty,0) for all values of gx​y2>gz2g_{xy}^{2}>g_{z}^{2}. Most importantly, on the isotropic axis gx​y2=gz2g_{xy}^{2}=g_{z}^{2}, there is a quantum critical fixed point QCPIsing{}_{\text{Ising}} that governs a continuous transition between Ising order and the disordered phase for 0<ϵ<ϵc0<\epsilon<\epsilon_{\mathrm{c}} and between the Ising order and XY order phase for ϵc<ϵ<1/2\epsilon_{\mathrm{c}}<\epsilon<1/2. For ϵ\epsilon above, but not too far from ϵc\epsilon_{\mathrm{c}}, the two-loop flow equations thus suggest a continuous order-to-order transition governed by the QCPIsing{}_{\text{Ising}} fixed point. In fact, the qualitative picture indicated by the perturbative calculation has recently been confirmed in large-scale numerical calculations [46, 47]; see also Refs. [44, 111] for recent analytical approaches based on large-SS expansions. The numerical calculations show that the true critical value of the control parameter ϵ\epsilon, at which the quantum critical fixed point QCPXY{}_{\text{XY}} and the infrared stable fixed point D collide, is ϵc=0.2294​(1)\epsilon_{\mathrm{c}}=0.2294(1), and thus close to our perturbative estimate. Interestingly, the numerical data for the transition between the Ising and XY ordered phases (see Fig. 9(d) of Ref. [47]) confirm our theoretical predictions for a continuous order-to-order transition from fixed-point annihilation, as formulated in the main text: First, on the XY side of the transition, the corresponding order parameter is significantly suppressed in comparison with its counterpart on the Ising side. Second, finite-temperature effects are significantly more enhanced on the XY side of the transition. Both properties can be understood as direct consequence of the annihilation between the QCPXY{}_{\text{XY}} and D fixed points and the resulting slow flow on the XY side of the transition.

D.2 Quantum chromodynamics with four-fermion interactions

As an example for a continuous order-to-order transition relevant to high-energy physics, we discuss quantum chromodynamics in 3+13+1 space-time dimensions (QCD4), supplemented with local four-fermion interactions, defined by the action [112, 61, 63, 64, 60, 65]

SQCD4-GN=∫d4x⁡[ⅈ​ψ¯​D̸​ψ+14​Fzμ​ν​Fμ​νz+12​∑α=14Gα​𝒪α]\displaystyle S_{\text{QCD${}_{4}$-GN}}=\int\hskip-2.5pt\differential[4]{x}\left[\rmi\bar{\psi}\not{D}\psi+\frac{1}{4}F_{z}^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}^{z}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{4}G_{\alpha}\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}\right] (74)

with covariant derivative D̸≔γμ(∂μ−ⅈgAμ)\not{D}\coloneqq\gamma_{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}-\rmi gA_{\mu}), SU(NcolorN_{\text{color}}) gauge field Aμ≔Aμz​TzA_{\mu}\coloneqq A_{\mu}^{z}T^{z}, and the associated field-strength tensor Fμ​ν≔Fμ​νz​TzF_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq F_{\mu\nu}^{z}T^{z}, where TzT^{z} denote the generators of SU(Ncolor)(N_{\text{color}}). A Fierz-complete basis of local four-fermion interactions is given by [112]

𝒪1\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{1} ≔(ψ¯a​γμ​ψb)2+(ψ¯a​γμ​γ5​ψb)2,\displaystyle\coloneqq\left(\bar{\psi}^{a}\gamma_{\mu}\psi^{b}\right)^{2}+\left(\bar{\psi}^{a}\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}\psi^{b}\right)^{2}, (75)
𝒪2\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{2} ≔(ψ¯a​ψb)2−(ψ¯a​γ5​ψb)2,\displaystyle\coloneqq\left(\bar{\psi}^{a}\psi^{b}\right)^{2}-\left(\bar{\psi}^{a}\gamma_{5}\psi^{b}\right)^{2}, (76)
𝒪3,4\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{3,4} ≔(ψ¯​γμ​ψ)2±(ψ¯​γμ​γ5​ψ)2.\displaystyle\coloneqq\left(\bar{\psi}\gamma_{\mu}\psi\right)^{2}\pm\left(\bar{\psi}\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}\psi\right)^{2}. (77)

For notational simplicity, we have abbreviated ψ¯​ψ≡ψ¯ia​ψia\bar{\psi}\psi\equiv\bar{\psi}_{i}^{a}\psi_{i}^{a} and (ψ¯a​ψb)2≡ψ¯ia​ψib​ψ¯jb​ψja(\bar{\psi}^{a}\psi^{b})^{2}\equiv\bar{\psi}^{a}_{i}\psi^{b}_{i}\bar{\psi}^{b}_{j}\psi^{a}_{j}, and assumed summation convention over repeated color indices i,ji,j and flavor indices a,ba,b. Consider the so-called Veneziano limit Nflavor,Ncolor→∞N_{\text{flavor}},N_{\text{color}}\rightarrow\infty with fixed ratio x≔Nflavor/Ncolorx\coloneqq N_{\text{flavor}}/N_{\text{color}}. In this limit, the flow equations reduce to a set of three equations [64, 60, 65],

ⅆg2ⅆln⁡b\displaystyle\frac{\rmd g^{2}}{\rmd\ln b} =2​(11−2​x)3​g4+2​(34−13​x)3​g6\displaystyle=\frac{2(11-2x)}{3}g^{4}+\frac{2(34-13x)}{3}g^{6}
−2​x​g4​G1,\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt-2xg^{4}G_{1}, (78)
ⅆG1ⅆln⁡b\displaystyle\frac{\rmd G_{1}}{\rmd\ln b} =−2​G1−(1+x)​G12−x4​G22+34​g4,\displaystyle=-2G_{1}-(1+x)G_{1}^{2}-\frac{x}{4}G_{2}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}g^{4}, (79)
ⅆG2ⅆln⁡b\displaystyle\frac{\rmd G_{2}}{\rmd\ln b} =−2​G2+2​G22−2​x​G1​G2+6​g2​G2+92​g4,\displaystyle=-2G_{2}+2G_{2}^{2}-2xG_{1}G_{2}+6g^{2}G_{2}+\frac{9}{2}g^{4}, (80)

where we have rescaled the gauge coupling g2​Ncolor/(16​π2)↦g2g^{2}N_{\text{color}}/(16\pi^{2})\mapsto g^{2} and the four-fermion couplings G1,2​Λ2​Ncolor/(4​π2)↦G1,2G_{1,2}\Lambda^{2}N_{\text{color}}/(4\pi^{2})\mapsto G_{1,2}. For reasons of consistency with the previous sections, we write the flow equations in terms of an RG scale ln⁡b\ln b, with ln⁡b=0\ln b=0 (ln⁡b→∞\ln b\to\infty) corresponding to the ultraviolet (infrared) scale.

The fixed-point structure of the model in the Veneziano limit is shown schematically in Fig. 14(a). For x>11/2x>11/2, asymptotic freedom is lost and the gauge coupling vanishes in the infrared if G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are small at the ultraviolet scale. For x<11/2x<11/2, the gauge charge is a RG relevant parameter and flows towards a finite value g2=g⋆2​(G1)=(11−2​x−3​x​G1)/(13​x−34)g^{2}=g^{2}_{\star}(G_{1})=({11-2x-3xG_{1}})/({13x-34}) in the infrared. For xx below, but not too far from 11/211/2, the infrared attractive plane g2=g⋆2​(G1)g^{2}=g^{2}_{\star}(G_{1}) hosts a fully infrared stable fixed point that can be associated with the conformal phase of many-flavor QCD4, the so-called Caswell-Banks-Zaks fixed point (CBZ) [113, 114]. In addition, the plane features two fixed points with unique infrared relevant directions, which can be associated to quantum critical points (QCP1 and QCP2). For decreasing xx, the infrared stable CBZ fixed point and one of the two quantum critical points (QCP2) approach each other and eventually collide at the critical value xc=4.05x_{\text{c}}=4.05. This is illustrated in Figs. 14(b)–(d), which show the RG flow in the plane g2=g⋆2​(G1)g^{2}=g^{2}_{\star}(G_{1}) for different values of xx. The runaway flow towards G2→+∞G_{2}\to+\infty at finite RG scale is usually associated with an instability towards a chiral symmetry breaking ground state [61, 42, 63]. The other quantum critical point (QCP1) in the infrared attractive plane g2=g⋆2​(G1)g^{2}=g^{2}_{\star}(G_{1}), however, is not affected by the fixed-point annihilation and persists for all x>0x>0. Since the runaway flow corresponding to this quantum critical fixed point is towards (G1,G2)→(−∞,−∞)(G_{1},G_{2})\to(-\infty,-\infty), one should expect it to describe an instability towards a different ground state, spontaneously breaking a symmetry different from chiral symmetry. This suggests a continuous order-to-order transition for x<xcx<x_{\text{c}} governed by QCP1.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
